questions.question: Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $0=A_0^n<A_1^n<\dots<A_n^n<A_{n+1}^n=1$ and spacings $X_k^n=A_k^n-A_{k-1}^n$, $k=1,\dots,n+1$. For $0<x<n$, when exactly is the first spacing $X_1^n=A_1^n$ larger than $x/n$?
options: When at least one of the $n$ points lies to the right of $x/n$.
When exactly one of the $n$ points lies inside the interval $[0,x/n]$.
When none of the $n$ points lies inside the interval $[0,x/n]$.
When the largest point $A_n^n$ lies to the right of $x/n$.

questions.question: Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $0=A_0^n<A_1^n<\dots<A_n^n<A_{n+1}^n=1$ and spacings $X_k^n=A_k^n-A_{k-1}^n$, $k=1,\dots,n+1$. The theorem states that $nX_k^n$ converges in distribution to $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$. What does this mean for a fixed $k$?
options: For every $x\ge0$, $\mathbb{P}(nX_k^n\le x)\to1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ as $n\to\infty$.
For all $n$ beyond some $n_0$, $nX_k^n$ is exactly $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ distributed.
The average of the $n+1$ scaled spacings $nX_k^n$ tends to an $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ variable.
Since $\mathbb{E}[nX_k^n]\to1$, the scaled spacing $nX_k^n$ tends to the constant $1$.

questions.question: Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $0=A_0^n<A_1^n<\dots<A_n^n<A_{n+1}^n=1$ and spacings $X_k^n=A_k^n-A_{k-1}^n$, $k=1,\dots,n+1$. Why does the theorem state a limit for $nX_k^n$ rather than for $X_k^n$ itself?
options: Because $X_k^n$ converges to $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ only after the dependence between spacings is removed.
Because $X_k^n$ tends to $0$; multiplying by $n$ measures the gap in units of the typical gap $1/n$.
Because multiplying by $n$ makes the $n+1$ scaled spacings sum to $1$, as a distribution requires.
Because $X_k^n$ has mean $1/n$ exactly, so $nX_k^n$ has mean exactly $1$ for every $n$.

questions.question: Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $0=A_0^n<A_1^n<\dots<A_n^n<A_{n+1}^n=1$ and spacings $X_k^n=A_k^n-A_{k-1}^n$, $k=1,\dots,n+1$. For a fixed finite $n$, are the spacings $X_1^n,\dots,X_{n+1}^n$ independent?
options: Yes, because they are built from the independent variables $U_1,\dots,U_n$.
Yes, because they all have the same density $n(1-r)^{n-1}$ on $(0,1)$.
Yes after scaling: the variables $nX_1^n,\dots,nX_{n+1}^n$ are independent.
No, because they always add up to $1$, so one long gap forces the others to be shorter.

questions.question: A hospital serves $n$ patients who each visit once per period, with independent phases uniform on the period. The planner merges all visits. For large $n$, which model describes the gaps between consecutive merged visits?
options: Exponential gaps of mean $1/n$ period, as in a Poisson process of rate $n$.
Gaps close to $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$, i.e. one merged visit per period on average.
Exponential gaps of mean $n$ periods, so the rate falls to $1/n$ per period.
Gaps spread evenly over $[0,2/n]$, which also gives a mean gap of $1/n$.

questions.question: Three i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ points fall at $0.55$, $0.15$ and $0.8$. With $A_0^3=0$ and $A_4^3=1$, what are the spacings $(X_1^3,X_2^3,X_3^3,X_4^3)$, where $X_k^3=A_k^3-A_{k-1}^3$?
options: $(0.4,\,0.25)$, the gaps between neighbouring points only
$(0.15,\,0.4,\,0.25)$, with no gap after the last point
$(0.15,\,0.4,\,0.25,\,0.2)$, including both end gaps
$(0.15,\,0.55,\,0.8,\,1)$, the sorted points and the end point

questions.question: Nine points $U_1,\dots,U_9$ are i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ and $A_9^9$ is the largest. What is the exact probability that the last spacing $X_{10}^9=1-A_9^9$ exceeds $0.1$?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.368$

questions.question: Four points are thrown independently and uniformly onto $[0,1]$, giving the spacings $X_1^4,\dots,X_5^4$ between $0$, the sorted points and $1$. What is the exact mean $\mathbb{E}[X_k^4]$ of a single spacing?
options: $1/4$, since four points give a mean gap of $1/n$
$4/5$, since a spacing has mean $n/(n+1)$
$1/3$, one third of the interval between the outer points
$1/5$, since five spacings share the unit interval

questions.question: A clinic has $200$ patients who each visit once a year, with independent phases uniform over the year. Using the exponential limit for the gap between consecutive merged visits, approximately what is the probability that a gap exceeds $1/100$ year?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.135$
$1-\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.865$
$\mathrm{e}^{-1}\approx0.368$
$\mathrm{e}^{-1/2}\approx0.607$

questions.question: Three points $U_1,U_2,U_3$ are i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $A_1^3<A_2^3<A_3^3$. Which function is the density on $(0,1)$ of the middle spacing $X_2^3=A_2^3-A_1^3$?

Fifty patients all start at time $0$ and plan their first visit uniformly in $[0.9,1.1]$, instead of having independent phases uniform on $[0,1]$. How do the gaps between the merged first visits compare with the exponential prediction of mean $1/50$?
options: They match it, because each patient's visit time is still uniform and independent of the others.
They are much shorter on average: the visits bunch in a window of length $0.2$, giving too many short gaps.
They are much longer on average: a narrow planning window spreads the visits apart from each other.
They have the same mean $1/50$, because the window is centred at the period $1$; only the spread of the gaps changes.

questions.question: Let $U_1,U_2$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1))$. The sum $U_1+U_2$ has a triangular density on $[0,2)$. What is the distribution of its fractional part $(U_1+U_2)\bmod 1$?
options: Triangular on $[0,1)$ with peak at $1/2$, since folding preserves the shape of the sum.
Concentrated near $0$, since the peak of the sum at $1$ folds back onto $0$.
Uniform on $[0,1/2)$, since it averages the two uniform phases.
Uniform on $[0,1)$, since the two folded pieces of the triangle add up to $1$.

questions.question: Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $0=A_0^n<A_1^n<\dots<A_n^n<A_{n+1}^n=1$ and spacings $X_k^n=A_k^n-A_{k-1}^n$, $k=1,\dots,n+1$. Since $nX_k^n\le n$ always, while an $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ variable is unbounded, why is $nX_k^n\to\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ in distribution still possible?
options: For each fixed $x$, eventually $n>x$, and the exponential tail beyond $n$ has probability $\mathrm{e}^{-n}\to0$.
Because the scaled spacings become independent, the bound $n$ on each of them disappears in the limit.
Because $\mathbb{E}[nX_k^n]=n/(n+1)$ is below $1$, the bound only affects the mean, not the distribution.
It is not possible; the limit holds only for $x\le1$, where the bound $n$ plays no role.

questions.question: Three points $U_1,U_2,U_3$ are i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $0=A_0^3<A_1^3<A_2^3<A_3^3<A_4^3=1$ and spacings $X_k^3=A_k^3-A_{k-1}^3$, $k=1,\dots,4$. Using the exact distribution of the scaled spacing $3X_k^3$, what is its median, i.e. the number $m$ with $\mathbb{P}(3X_k^3\le m)=1/2$?
options: $\ln 2\approx0.693$

questions.question: For $n=4$ i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ points, a spacing $X_k^4$ has density $4(1-r)^3$ on $(0,1)$. What is the value at $x=2$ of the density of the scaled spacing $4X_k^4$?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.135$

questions.question: A Poisson process with rate $\lambda=2$ has exactly $5$ arrivals in $[0,2]$. Given this, the arrival times are distributed as the order statistic of $5$ i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,2])$ variables. What is the expected gap between the second and third arrival?

Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $0=A_0^n<A_1^n<\dots<A_n^n<A_{n+1}^n=1$ and spacings $X_k^n=A_k^n-A_{k-1}^n$, $k=1,\dots,n+1$. Fix $x,y>0$ and let $n>x+y$. Which statement about the joint tail probability $\mathbb{P}(nX_1^n>x,\,nX_{n+1}^n>y)$ of the first and the last scaled spacing is correct?
options: It equals $(1-x/n)^n(1-y/n)^n$ for every such $n$: the first and the last gap lie at opposite ends of $[0,1]$, so they are independent already for finite $n$.
It equals $(1-(x+y)/n)^n$ and tends to $\mathrm{e}^{-(x+y)}$, which lies below the product $\mathrm{e}^{-x}\mathrm{e}^{-y}$ of the limiting tails: the dependence persists in the limit.
It equals $(1-(x+y)/n)^n$, below $(1-x/n)^n(1-y/n)^n$ for every such $n$, yet tends to $\mathrm{e}^{-x}\mathrm{e}^{-y}$: independence appears only in the limit.
It tends to $0$: the spacings sum to $1$, so two long gaps cannot occur together, and multiplying by $n$ does not lift this constraint as $n\to\infty$.

questions.question: Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$ with order statistic $0=A_0^n<A_1^n<\dots<A_n^n<A_{n+1}^n=1$ and spacings $X_k^n=A_k^n-A_{k-1}^n$, $k=1,\dots,n+1$. For fixed $n\ge1$ and $0<x<n$, how does $\mathbb{P}(nX_k^n\le x)=1-(1-x/n)^n$ compare with the limit $1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}$?
options: It is larger for every such $x$, since $1-y<\mathrm{e}^{-y}$ for $y\ne0$; scaled gaps tend to be shorter.
It is smaller for every such $x$, since finite-$n$ scaled gaps tend to be longer than exponential ones.
It is larger for small $x$ and smaller for large $x$, since the two densities cross each other.
It is smaller for small $x$ and larger for large $x$, since the exact law has bounded support $[0,n]$.

questions.question: A patient's visit day on a cycle of $C=6$ days follows $A_i=(A_{i-1}+X_i)\bmod 6$ with i.i.d. gaps $X_i$, each of two values with probability $1/2$. For which pair of gap values does $\mathbb{P}(A_k=i)\to1/6$ for every day $i$?

Two points $U_1,U_2$ are i.i.d. $\operatorname{Unif}([0,1])$, with spacings $X_1^2,X_2^2,X_3^2$. Each spacing satisfies $\mathbb{P}(X_k^2>1/2)=(1/2)^2$. What are $\mathbb{P}(X_1^2>1/2,\,X_2^2>1/2)$ and $\mathbb{P}(X_1^2>1/2)\,\mathbb{P}(X_2^2>1/2)$?
